raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old male presented to a general practitioner with pain in the left arm and legs, weakness, sore throat, and chills. He was diagnosed with pharyngitis and prescribed antibiotics and paracetamol. The next day he developed 38.5  C fever with intense diaphoresis and consulted with another general practitioner. The physician confirmed pharyngitis, endorsed symptomatic treatment but withdrew antibiotics. The patient remained febrile and weak for the next five days. Unsolicited and unsupervised laboratory tests were performed, including a rapid HIV-antibody test which was reported as non-reactive. He had had a rapid HIV test two months before the onset of symptoms, which was negative. The WBC count and general labs showed leukopenia (3.9 x 103/muL) with 42 % neutrophils (1.65 x 103/muL), 42 % lymphocytes (1.68 x 103/muL), 14 % Monocytes (0.58 x 103/muL) and platelets 107 x 103/muL. Total cholesterol 105 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 134 UI/L, aspartate aminotransferase 190 UI/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 307 UI/L.
Seven days after the beginning of symptoms, fever subdued, but malaise remained. Fearing an HIV-infection because of a previous history of risk behavior, the patient sought laboratory-based testing. A 4th Gen chemiluminescence HIV-test was performed and reported reactive. After this result, delivered without counseling, he requested further HIV testing in three different places the same day: 1) Public Health Care Provider in a primary care setting, where a 3rd Gen-rapid test reported non-reactive, 2) Public AIDS-Counseling Center where a 3rd Gen- rapid test reported non-reactive, and 3) an AIDS-NGO facility where two rapid tests (Genie-Fast HIV1/2 3rd- and ALERE HIV-Combo, 4th-Gen) were performed simultaneously, and both reported non-reactive. The next day, he asked for primary care consultation and underwent another rapid 3rd Gen-test, reported non-reactive.
In doubt, the patient returned to the laboratory where he first tested positive, and a new test reported reactive again. The primary care physician ordered a WB in a reference laboratory. The WB was negative, but the clinical and testing history rose suspicion. We suggested and performed a physical examination of the patient and found prominent cervical bilateral adenopathy. Following detailed anamnesis, the patient reported unprotected receptive sex with male partners A and B, respectively, eight and six weeks before the symptoms. As he first tested positive, he requested both partners to undergo the same laboratory-based testing, and both were reported negative. The only suspected infection source was non-consensual, unprotected sexual contact ten days before the beginning of symptoms. The referring primary care physician considered the WB-result a true negative. However, because of the two reactive lab-based tests, the clinical picture and anamnesis, we suggested a further 4th Gen test (Genscreen Ultra HIV, Biorad) in our reference laboratory, which was reactive. Thus, eleven days after the onset of symptoms, five rapid non-reactive tests, one negative WB, and three 4th Gen reactive tests, the patient was diagnosed with acute retroviral syndrome and ongoing seroconversion. He was referred to a Public Health Institution, where another lab-based 4th Gen test was reactive, and a quantitative HIV-1 RNA viral load test reported > 3,000,000 copies/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presenting with sore throat, fever up to 38.5 °C, chills, intense diaphoresis, left arm and leg pain, and weakness for seven days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 29-year-old male presented with acute sore throat, chills, myalgias in the left arm and lower extremities, and generalized weakness. Over the following 24 hours, he developed high-grade fevers reaching 38.5 °C with profuse diaphoresis. He was initially diagnosed with pharyngitis and received empiric antibiotics and antipyretics, but high fever and severe asthenia persisted for five days. Although fever abated by day 7, persistent malaise and weakness prompted extensive evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior negative rapid serological screening tests, most recently 2 months prior to symptom onset. Epidemiological risk history: Unprotected receptive anal intercourse with two male partners 8 and 6 weeks prior to symptom onset (both partners tested negative); history of non-consensual unprotected sexual contact 10 days before symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Sore throat, chills, intense diaphoresis, pain in left arm and legs, generalized weakness, and persistent malaise.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination: Prominent bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy; pharyngeal erythema (initial general practitioner evaluation).
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukopenia of 3.9 x 10^3/muL (neutrophils 42% [1.65 x 10^3/muL], lymphocytes 42% [1.68 x 10^3/muL], monocytes 14% [0.58 x 10^3/muL]), thrombocytopenia of 107 x 10^3/muL. Serum biochemistry: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 134 UI/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 190 UI/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 307 UI/L, total cholesterol 105 mg/dL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute retroviral syndrome (ARS) secondary to acute human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection with early window-period seroconversion.
Confirmatory Testing & Diagnostic Trajectory: Patient exhibited discordant serologic results due to the early seroconversion window: five point-of-care rapid antibody tests (including 3rd-generation rapid tests and ALERE HIV-Combo) were falsely non-reactive, and standard Western blot (WB) was negative. Diagnosis was confirmed by repeated 4th-generation chemiluminescent antigen/antibody assays (reactive on initial lab-based assay, repeat assay, and Genscreen Ultra HIV Bio-Rad reference assay) and quantitative plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load demonstrating > 3,000,000 copies/mL.
Disposition & Plan: The patient was referred to a specialized public health institution for immediate linkage to care and initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy.
